catalog_quote: The basic syllable structure for Zaiwa can be represented as C1(C2)V(X) where X is optional vowel length (non-contrastive), a second member of a diphthong (V) or a final consonant (C3). Zaiwa also has unstressed, open, reduced CV syllables word initially, with a tendency towards vowel reduction to a [ə], e.g. [lədʒâŋ] ‘prepare’. Zaiwa is a tonal language with voice quality contrast between modal and tense phonation types. There are four tones marked as high-falling ( ˆ), high ( ´), mid (unmarked), and low . Tone in checked syllables is predictable from the voicing of the initial consonant and the presence or absence of tense phonation. If the initial consonant is voiced the tone is low. If the initial consonant is voiceless the tone is high. If the syllable has tense phonation the tone is high.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Zaiwa is not in the catalog. Both bibliography items are the same work (Wannemacher's 1996 UTA MA thesis and its 1998 SIL/UTA publication, 'Aspects of Zaiwa prosody: an autosegmental account'), and both are about word-level stress in Zaiwa. No open full text is reachable: the SIL archive (which holds per Glottolog) and HathiTrust/UTA repositories sit behind an automated-access block challenges by automated download, the Internet Archive/archive.org/OpenLibrary/Semantic Scholar/CORE have nothing, Google Books has no preview, and Thurgood's 2000 Language review is JSTOR-paywalled. Google Books search-inside snippets (saved as XML + digest under nonetheless yield the substantive statement: stress = syllable weight ([+stress] = μμ, [-stress] = μ); full syllables are stressed by default, reduced CV prefixes and suffixes are unstressed; correlates are intensity, vowel quality and length, not pitch; tone is the lexical prosody and interacts with stress only under emotional emphasis (§6.7 'Stress and tone', p. 112). Reading for the catalog: no positional or contrastive word stress; weight-driven full-vs-reduced prominence in a tone language. Acquiring the SIL PDF (sil_id 39216) is the high-priority follow-up; the 1996 thesis is low priority since the 1998 book supersedes it.

Zaiwa also has unstressed, open, reduced CV syllables word initially, with a tendency towards vowel reduction to a [ə], e.g. [lədʒâŋ] 'prepare'." followed by a new paragraph "Zaiwa is a tonal language with voice quality contrast between modal and tense phonation ty…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Zaiwa is a tone language (four lexical tones, three in some varieties; tone predictable in checked syllables). The only stress statement is negative/positional: word-initial reduced open CV (sesquisyllabic prefix) syllables are unstressed and reduce to [ə], so prominence sits on the full tone-bearing (word-final) syllable; no positive rule of word stress is given. Lustig 2010 (snippets, not opened) treats 'stress' as an emphatic morpho-phonological tone change (stressed syllable takes tone /55/, a following syllable weakens to /11/; §7.1 Stress, p. 157), e.g. in name-calling or clause-initial emphasis - i.e. not a fixed word-level stress position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Wannemacher 2010 fn 4: some varieties have only three tones; fn 11: in polysyllabic words tone is orthographically marked only on the last syllable. Lustig (snippet): 'stressing' = tone raised to /55/ with weakening of a second syllable to /11/, used in calling names and for emphasis (e.g. nang31 pronounced [nɐŋ52]); reduced-syllable lexical tone raising in allegro speech.
new_statements.domain_note: Wannemacher: word level (word-initial reduced syllables unstressed). Lustig's stress statements concern utterance-level emphasis/vocative calling ('stressed syllable is the first syllable of the clause') realised as tone change, which is phrase/morpho-phonological rather than lexical word stress. JIPA 2025 (Ruili speaker) and Dai 2026 (Hounong) give tone systems only and are silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Zaiwa proper (zaiw1241; no dialect glottocodes exist). Wannemacher 2010 describes the Myanmar (Kachin State, Janshi-area) variety in the Myitkyina-committee orthography with four tones (fn 4: some varieties have three); the JIPA 2025 illustration is a Ruili County speaker (Longzhun dialect, China) with six tones; Lustig 2010 is Dehong (China) Zaiwa; Dai 2026 is Hounong; Xu & Xu 1984 Xishan/Bengwa; Zhu 2013/2017 Zhefang.

new_statements.quote: Zaiwa word-level stress is appropriate since stress is relevant in determining syllable structure. Stress is manifest as acoustic intensity, full vowel quality, and vowel length and does not necessarily correspond to pitch. 59 Zaiwa stressed syllables are the unmarked case. Unstressed syllables are the marked case, occurring with peripheral syllables, and show vowel shortening and vowel reduction to [ə] word initially and word internally. Suffixes generally occur as unstressed syllables, but the vowel is not reduced. [...] Heavy and light syllables in Zaiwa correspond to stressed and unstressed syllables, respectively. [...] (78) [+stress] = μμ [-stress] = μ
new_statements.citation: Wannemacher, Mark W. 1998. Aspects of Zaiwa prosody: an autosegmental account. SIL and UTA Publications in Linguistics 129. Dallas: SIL.
new_statements.locator: Google Books search-inside snippets (vol. 6CJZAAAAMAAJ): syllable-structure chapter, passage ending at footnote 59, and the heavy/light passage on pp. 69-70 (running head '70 Aspects of Zaiwa Prosody' inside the snippet); constraint (78); TOC gives §6.7 'Stress and tone' at p. 112. Page images were not opened; text is verbatim snippet scanned stitched at '[..]'.
new_statements.reading: Zaiwa is a tone language with no positional word-stress rule. What Wannemacher calls stress is syllable weight: every full (bimoraic) syllable is stressed by default; the only unstressed syllables are reduced sesquisyllabic CV prefixes (schwa, word-initial/internal) and suffixes. In a prefix+root (sesquisyllabic) word the prominence therefore falls on the full root syllable; stress is realised by intensity, vowel quality and length, not pitch, and interacts with tone only under emotional emphasis (§6.7). For a catalog's classification: 'no lexical/contrastive word stress; weight-driven full-vs-reduced syllable prominence in a tonal language'. Consistent with the previously collected Wannemacher 2010 (LTBA) note on unstressed reduced initial CV syllables and with Lustig 2010's treatment of 'stress' as a morphophonological tone-raising process rather than lexical stress.

sources.note: Snippets (verbatim scanned, stitched from several queries) give a consistent picture: in Wannemacher's account 'stress' in Zaiwa is a syllable-weight property, not a positional word-stress rule. Full (heavy, bimoraic: long vowel/diphthong, or vowel + coda) syllables are stressed and are the unmarked case; unstressed syllables are the marked case = reduced sesquisyllabic CV prefixes (vowel shortened to [ə]) word-initially/internally and suffixes (unstressed but unreduced). Formalised as '(78) [+stress] = μμ, [-stress] = μ'. Stress correlates are intensity, full vowel quality and vowel length,…
